opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the data piece is underrated because people tend to frame the US–China AI race almost entirely around compute: chips, export controls, how many GPUs each side can get. That matters a lot, but a frontier model is also shaped by the data you put into post-training, and that's where the ecosystems look quite different.

In the US, there's now a real industry built around producing training data for frontier labs: Scale AI, Surge, Mercor, Turing, and a long tail of smaller vendors. These companies recruit people with real expertise, like PhD mathematicians, software engineers, doctors, and lawyers. They pay them well to write very hard prompts, carefully graded responses, preference comparisons, and now increasingly reinforcement learning environments and rubrics. The labs spend enormous amounts on this, plausibly billions of dollars a year in aggregate. That money buys you something hard to replicate: a steady supply of high-quality human signal for the exact behaviors you want, like reasoning through a tricky proof, using tools correctly in an agentic workflow, or writing code that matches how professionals actually work.

In China, as far as I can tell, that market is much less mature. There's plenty of labeling labor, and historically a lot of it supported computer vision and autonomous driving. But the high-end, expert-heavy, post-training-specific data business isn't nearly as developed. The Chinese labs are extremely talented, and they've compensated in clever ways. They lean heavily on synthetic data, on distillation from strong models, and on reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where you can check answers automatically in math and code instead of needing a human to judge every output. DeepSeek's work is a good example of how far you can get with that recipe.

The reason it matters is that verifiable domains are only part of what people want from these models. Once you move into fuzzier territory, like writing quality, nuanced instruction following, professional judgment, character, and long-horizon agentic tasks in messy real-world software, you need human expertise to define what "good" looks like. That's where a deep data-vendor ecosystem gives American labs an edge that doesn't show up in benchmark tables right away, but does show up in how the models feel to use and how well they generalize to real work.

So I'd put it this way: Chinese labs have shown they can be very efficient and close the gap on capabilities you can measure cheaply. The data industry gap is one of the structural reasons the last mile of polish and real-world usefulness could stay harder for them, at least until that ecosystem catches up. It's also a reminder that the race isn't only about hardware. A lot of the moat is in the unglamorous, expensive work of figuring out exactly what you want the model to do and paying people to show it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a mature US training-data vendor ecosystem and says China’s high-end market is less developed, but it does not state that buying data from suppliers is standard in US labs and rare among Chinese companies.

r002.rationale: It discusses producing human signal for desired behaviors, but does not identify purchasing data tailored to a model’s specific weaknesses as a performance-improvement method.

r003.rationale: It says Chinese labs are efficient and can close gaps on measurable capabilities, but does not suggest this reflects their choosing different problems from American labs.

r004.rationale: The suggestion that China’s ecosystem may catch up implies the gap could change, but the response does not state that the difference is not inherently necessary between the countries.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the thing people miss when they compare the two ecosystems is that training a frontier model today is not really a compute problem alone, it's a data problem. And specifically it's a post-training data problem. Pretraining data you can mostly scrape. But the stuff that actually makes a model good — the instruction data, the preference data, the reasoning traces, the agentic trajectories — a lot of that is produced by people. Expert annotators, contractors, domain specialists writing and grading examples.

In the US, that has become a real industry. Scale AI, Surge, Mercor, Handshake, a bunch of others — these are companies with hundreds of millions or billions in revenue whose entire business is sourcing PhDs and software engineers and doctors to produce very high-quality labeled data for the labs. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta all spend enormous amounts on this. It's one of the biggest line items after compute, and it's quietly a big part of why the top American models are as polished as they are.

When I look at China, that layer is much thinner. There are data labeling companies, sure, but they historically grew up around autonomous driving and computer vision — bounding boxes, relatively low-skill annotation. The high-end, expert-in-the-loop, pay-a-lawyer-to-write-preference-data market just hasn't matured the same way. Part of it is money: the Chinese labs operate on much smaller budgets, so they can't write the kinds of checks that make that market exist. Part of it is that the talent you'd want doing this work is expensive and has other options.

And the interesting consequence is that it shapes how Chinese labs do research. If you can't buy a million expert-written samples, you lean harder on synthetic data, on distillation from stronger models, on reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards where you don't need a human grader at all. DeepSeek is a great example — a lot of their cleverness is in squeezing more out of algorithms and automated pipelines precisely because they didn't have the data budget. So in some ways the constraint has made them more efficient and more creative.

But I think it still shows up as a gap. The things that are hardest to get right without humans in the loop — tone, judgment, handling messy real-world tasks, the "feel" of a model — that's where the US models tend to be ahead, and I attribute a lot of that to the data industry rather than to raw compute or smarter researchers. It's an underappreciated piece of infrastructure, and it's the one I'd watch to see whether that gap closes or widens.

r001.rationale: It describes a mature US market of companies that source expert-produced data and says major US labs spend heavily on it, while China’s corresponding high-end data market is much thinner.

r002.rationale: It discusses expert data and its effects, but does not say labs can target data purchases at a model’s specific weaknesses.

r003.rationale: It attributes Chinese labs’ efficiency to constraints that drive synthetic data, distillation, and automated methods, but does not suggest they choose different problems from American labs.

r004.rationale: It names budget and talent as causes and says the gap may close or widen, but does not state that the industry difference is not inherently necessary between the countries.

astra-6.text:
I think it matters because a lot of what makes an AI model useful happens after the initial pretraining. You need people to write good examples, compare responses, and judge whether a model is actually doing the task well. That takes an industry capable of finding people with the right expertise and organizing their work into reliable training data.

If that industry is less developed in China, then an AI lab has to build more of that infrastructure itself. You can have talented researchers and access to compute, but turning those resources into a consistently useful assistant becomes harder. And as the tasks become more specialized—coding, mathematics, scientific reasoning—the quality of the people producing and evaluating that data matters even more.

So I see it as an ecosystem difference, rather than a fundamental limitation on Chinese researchers. It’s something that can change, but it takes time to build.

r001.rationale: The response discusses China’s less-developed data infrastructure but does not say external suppliers are standard for U.S. labs and rare for Chinese companies.

r002.rationale: It discusses producing and evaluating training data, but not purchasing data tailored to a model’s specific weaknesses.

r003.rationale: It does not compare startup efficiency or suggest Chinese startups choose different problems from U.S. labs.

r004.rationale: It calls the difference an ecosystem issue rather than a fundamental limitation on Chinese researchers, and says it can change over time.

sol-6.1.text:
Because training data isn’t just something you download from the internet anymore. A lot of the work in making a model useful comes from getting people to write good examples, compare responses, and evaluate whether the model actually did the task correctly. That takes infrastructure: finding the right people, managing the work, and checking quality.

If that industry is less developed, an AI lab has to build more of that capability internally. You can have strong researchers and access to compute, but it’s harder to run a fast cycle where you train a model, identify its weaknesses, collect targeted data, and improve it.

So I see it as an ecosystem difference, rather than a difference in talent. And it’s something that can change. But access to a mature data industry can make a big difference in how quickly a lab turns a capable base model into a useful product.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data-work infrastructure but does not say that American frontier labs commonly buy training data while Chinese companies rarely do.

r002.rationale: It describes identifying model weaknesses, collecting targeted data, and using it to improve the model.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss Chinese startups’ apparent efficiency or suggest they may be working on different problems from American labs.

r004.rationale: It describes the difference as an ecosystem issue that can change, communicating that it is not an inherent or fixed difference between the countries.
